name: Obsidian Addendum
description: Obsidian Addendum is a tiny, airless rock that orbits at the outer edge of a binary star system, its surface a record of every impact it has endured over billions of years. Craters overlap craters in a palimpsest of destruction, their floors glazed with impact glass that has fused into smooth, dark plains reflecting the distant twin suns. The temperature swings wildly depending on which sun—or both—is above the horizon, creating thermal stress fractures that slowly shatter the glass plains into angular shards.

Without atmosphere, the surface exists in absolute silence. The only motion is the imperceptible creep of thermal expansion and contraction, the slow settling of impact debris, and the occasional new strike from the system's dense asteroid belt. The twin suns cast double shadows that shift in complex patterns across the glass plains, creating an effect that early surveyors described as watching two hands write simultaneously on the same dark page.

A satellite graveyard occupies a stable orbit above the equator—dozens of defunct probes, relay stations, and navigational buoys from at least three different eras of exploration, all drawn into the same orbital slot by the moonlet's surprisingly regular gravitational field. The oldest satellites date back centuries, their designs unfamiliar and their data cores encrypted in formats no longer in common use. Someone—or several someones—found this unremarkable rock worth watching for a very long time.

Obsidian Addendum's only strategic value is its position at the intersection of three navigational corridors, making it a useful waypoint for course corrections. The satellite graveyard has attracted salvagers, but the encrypted data cores have drawn intelligence operatives who believe the oldest satellites may contain star charts to regions of space that have since been declared off-limits. For a world that appears to be nothing more than a footnote in a binary system's history, it has accumulated a surprising number of secrets in its orbit.
